content.title: Data Science Techniques for Energy Analysis

content.text: Lesson 1 Overview

The evolving complexity of modern energy systems—shaped by climate imperatives, technological innovation, and accessibility challenges—demands analytical approaches capable of navigating unprecedented data volumes and interdependencies. This lesson examines how contemporary methodologies are transforming energy analysis from descriptive diagnostics toward predictive and prescriptive capabilities.

We explore how advanced techniques uncover hidden patterns within energy consumption, distribution anomalies, and demand drivers, enabling more resilient infrastructure 💬️ planning. The discussion extends to spatial intelligence applications, demonstrating how integrated geospatial and remote sensing data enhance environmental stewardship, renewable asset optimization, and equitable resource allocation. Critically, we consider the role of intuitive data translation in bridging technical insights and actionable strategies—ensuring analytical rigor serves both operational efficiency and community-centric solutions.

Across these domains, emphasis remains on practical implementation: how data science not only illuminates energy system behaviors but also navigates real-world constraints. Case examples from diverse operational contexts will highlight trade-offs between innovation scalability and contextual adaptation, setting a grounded foundation for evaluating data-driven opportunities in pursuit of sustainability and accessibility goals.

content.title: Key Concepts
content.intro: Explore foundational ideas from this lesson.

concepts.title: data visualization
concepts.body: Data visualization is the graphical representation of information and data, using visual elements like charts, graphs, and maps to make complex data more accessible and understandable.

concepts.title: exploratory data analysis (eda)
concepts.body: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is an approach to analyzing data sets to summarize their main characteristics, often using visual methods, before applying formal modeling or hypothesis testing.

concepts.title: geographical information system (gis)
concepts.body: A Geographical Information System (GIS) is a technology that captures, stores, analyzes, and presents spatial or geographic data, allowing users to visualize and interpret data related to locations on Earth.

content.title: A: Statistical Modeling for Energy Systems

content.text: One type of EDA, multivariate graphical, displays relationships in data sets by using graphics such as scatter plots, histograms, bar charts, box plots, and heat maps. These visualizations help identify trends, such as seasonal variations in energy usage or inefficiencies in energy distribution networks. The following figure illustrates steps used in exploratory data analysis.

Data science uses various techniques to extract insights from raw data. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is a technique for uncovering patterns, and identifying anomalies (e.g., missing values and outliers) and patterns within the data. It can be used to validate preprocessing steps, ensuring data readiness for further analysis and modelling. For instance, EDA might show a strong correlation between temperature and energy usage, highlighting temperature as a significant predictor of energy demand.

EDA traditionally demands a significant amount of time and expertise. However, A.I. has streamlined this process, making it more efficient and accurate. A.I. algorithms can rapidly process vast amounts of data, detecting errors and outliers to clean and transform data more efficiently and accurately than human analysts. Additionally, A.I. is capable of managing diverse and complex datasets, including text, images, and high-dimensional data. By automating much of the EDA process, A.I. can potentially enable data analysts to explore and comprehend their data more quickly and effectively .
Automating data cleaning

One of the critical stages in EDA is data cleaning, which involves handling missing values and duplicates, correcting errors, and formatting data. A.I. can significantly improve this process through automated data cleaning techniques. Machine learning models can learn from historical data cleaning tasks and apply these learnings to new datasets, reducing the time and effort required for data preparation. For example, A.I.-driven tools can automatically detect and impute missing values, ensuring that the dataset is as complete and accurate as possible before analysis.
Clustering and anomaly detection

A.I. algorithms, such as k-means clustering and autoencoders, play a niche role in anomaly detection during EDA. These algorithms can automatically group data points into clusters based on their similarities, identify underlying patterns in, for example, energy consumption, production, and distribution . Autoencoders, a type of neural network, can detect anomalies by learning the normal behavior of energy systems and flagging data points that deviate significantly from this norm. For example, autoencoders can identify irregular spikes in energy usage that might indicate equipment malfunctions or unauthorized energy consumption, enabling timely interventions to prevent potential issues .
Pattern recognition and prediction

Machine learning algorithms enhance EDA by enabling sophisticated pattern recognition and prediction capabilities. Algorithms like k-nearest neighbor, decision trees, random forests, and support vector machines are particularly effective in classifying and predicting energy usage patterns. By analyzing historical data, these algorithms can identify trends and correlations that might not be immediately apparent. For instance, pattern recognition can assist in predicting daily or seasonal energy demand by identifying consumption patterns related to weather conditions, time of day, or day of the week. This capability allows utility companies to optimize their operations, plan for peak demand periods, and improve the overall efficiency of energy distribution .

content.title: Case Study: India
content.subtitle: Slashing $18B post-harvest losses with Solar-Powered cold rooms and AI – empowering women-led farmer cooperatives through Pay-Per-Use cooling and digital market access in India and beyond

content.text:
India’s agricultural sector faces substantial challenges, including significant post-harvest losses. Recent studies estimate that India suffers food losses worth approximately USD17.7–18.5 billion annually (ICRIER, 2024; National Economic Forum, 2025), with fruits and vegetables experiencing losses of 30–35% due to inadequate cold chain infrastructure. Approximately 74 million tonnes of food are lost in India each year, accounting for 22% of the foodgrain output (PMF IAS, 2024), resulting in significant income loss for smallholder farmers.

To address these challenges, the ‘Your Virtual Cold Chain Assistant’ (Your VCCA) initiative was launched in 2021 by BASE and Empa. The initiative leverages decentralized, solar-powered cold storage facilities to help small-scale farmers and aggregators access affordable cooling solutions through a Cooling-as-a-Service (CaaS) model (Your VCCA).

content.title: 2023-2024
content.body: Expansion to Nigeria and the Philippines, with app testing and enhancement of features, including farmers’ interface.

content.title: Current Status
content.body: Integration of impact dashboard for tracking utilization rates, revenue growth, and post-harvest loss reduction.

content.title: 2022
content.body: Pilot demonstrations in Bihar and Himachal Pradesh, with data collection and user testing.

content.text: The Your Virtual Cold Chain Assistant (Your VCCA) initiative followed a structured three-phase implementation approach, progressing from initial pilot testing to broader scale-up and impact assessment across multiple countries.
Methodology
Phase 1: Technology Development and Digital Innovation (2021)

The foundational element of the VCCA initiative is its robust digitalization strategy, centered around the Coldtivate Mobile App. This application leverages Machine Learning (ML) and physics-based food modeling to estimate the precise storage life of produce, optimize inventory management, and provide real-time temperature monitoring within cold rooms . Furthermore, it offers crucial market price forecasts, enabling farmers to make informed decisions about when and where to sell their crops to maximize returns (BASE and Empa, 2022). Recognizing the digital divide, SMS notifications ensure accessibility for farmers without smartphones, bridging critical information gaps (SEforAll, 2024).

Complementing the digital tools is the innovative Cooling-as-a-Service (CaaS) model, where solar-powered cold rooms are strategically deployed on a pay-per-use basis, effectively eliminating prohibitive upfront costs for smallholders. Real-time IoT monitoring ensures the efficient operation of these cold rooms and preserves crop quality. These facilities are located in accessible public spaces, as demonstrated by the cold room built near the bustling VSS Market in Rourkela, Odisha, ensuring accessibility for local farmers (SEforAll, 2024).
Phase 2: Pilot and Early Expansion (2021–2022)

The initiative commenced with a pilot phase in Bihar and Himachal Pradesh during 2021–2022, designed to demonstrate the economic viability of the CaaS business model and the value-add of the VCCA app (Climate Finance Lab, 2022). BASE and Empa began working towards addressing post-harvest challenges in January 2021 under the Your VCCA initiative as part of the data.org global innovation challenge.

After a year and a half of interdisciplinary teamwork including strong local partnership development, data collection, user interface design, and the development of machine learning and physics-based models, the team released the first version of its data-science-based mobile application called Coldtivate (BASE and Empa, 2022, para. 3).

Capacity Building and gender mainstreaming 💬️ were integral from the outset, with partnerships established with local organizations, such as women’s self-help groups, to manage the cold storage facilities. This approach not only ensured cultural accessibility but also provided digital skills training for women in operations and finance. By fostering women’s leadership in cold room management, the initiative helped build community trust and enhance the long-term sustainability of the model (SEforAll, 2024, para. 4).
Phase 3: Full Implementation and Impact Assessment (2023–2024)

The project entered its complete implementation phase with Coldtivate being tested in 21 cold rooms across India, Nigeria, and the Philippines. This replaces manual registries, ensuring that all cold chain actors have access to reliable, up-to-date information and market intelligence (Your VCCA-Coldtivate).

A critical component of this phase is the collection of gender-disaggregated data through built-in surveys in the app, which are used to calculate statistics on the evolution of post-harvest loss and income for women and men farmers separately. BASE and Empa plan to combine this information with farmers’ utilization and payment patterns in an exportable impact dashboard to help farmers access microcredits and other financial services (SEforAll, 2024).
Outcomes and Impact

content.body: Farmer revenues are projected to increase by more than 35% with cold storage implementation.
Waste reduction from 25% to 5% for stored commodities.
Price realization improvement from INR 40/kg to INR 88/kg for apples through off-season selling.
Project IRR of 22.5% and Equity IRR of 31.1% for cold storage projects.
Physics-based digital twins for predicting mass loss and shelf-life of stored fruits.
Climate-friendly cooling solutions enabled by CaaS can reduce GHG emissions by up to 50% and support food security by reducing food spoilage by more than 30%.
Projected cumulative impact within four years includes benefiting 1.5 million farmers, abating 100,000 tonnes of CO2, and mobilizing USD 200 million in cold room projects.

content.text: The ‘Your VCCA’ initiative in India offers profound lessons for sustainable development through digitalization, particularly for regions confronting similar agricultural and energy challenges:

content.title: Empowering Local Communities
content.body: Robust community engagement and gender mainstreaming were foundational, with partnerships with women’s self-help groups and digital skills training ensuring local ownership and enhanced sustainability of the cold storage facilities (SEforAll, 2024). This approach not only improved livelihoods but also strengthened social equity.

content.title: Integrated Digital Solutions
content.body: The success underscores the power of combining innovative business models (CaaS) with accessible digital tools (Coldtivate app, SMS notifications). These tools were crucial in bridging the digital divide and enabling real-time data-driven decision-making for farmers (BASE and Empa, 2022). The continuous data collection from IoT sensors and the app feeds into refining operational efficiency and market trends.

content.title: Scalable and Climate-Resilient Model
content.body: The CaaS model demonstrates significant climate and scalability benefits, with climate-friendly cooling solutions that reduce GHG emissions by 50% and support food security by reducing food spoilage by more than 30%. The model’s success has been replicated across multiple contexts, with 100% solar-powered walk-in cold rooms implemented in farm clusters, produce aggregation centers, and outdoor markets, and expansion documented in India, Nigeria, and the Philippines, demonstrating its adaptability for scaling clean energy adoption in agricultural supply chains.

content.title: Data for Adaptive Management and Policy
content.body: The app enables cooling beneficiaries to track crop quality in storage in real time, empowering farmers to make informed decisions on when and where to sell their crops. Furthermore, the gender-disaggregated impact data-informed program refinement and demonstrated tangible, gender-equitable outcomes. The project’s data on storage optimization serves as evidence for future program design and funding.

In the face of pressing environmental issues, such as climate change, deforestation, and pollution source identification, advancements in Artificial Intelligence (A.I.) enhance the usefulness and power of geospatial data analytics. Decision-makers can leverage data tools to assess the impacts and siting of low-carbon energy resources and associated infrastructure. A.I.’s exceptional computational power and data processing capabilities make it a vital tool in the effort to preserve and protect our planet .

Sirmacek and Vinuesa (2022) explored the integration of A.I. and remote sensing 💬️ to enhance climate adaptation in urban areas. They proposed a framework combining A.I. and simulation to extract indicators from satellite images, facilitating predictive estimations of future states related to climate adaptation. Their study highlighted the potential of A.I. to create rapid land-use maps, simulate disaster scenarios, identify outliers, and provide real-time predictions. This approach aims to aid decision-makers in sustaining societal well-being, natural resources, and biodiversity.

Remote sensing and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) have become indispensable tools in the energy sector, providing comprehensive and precise data and analysis about spatial relationships. Remote sensing encompasses technologies that capture data about the Earth's surface from a distance, typically through satellites, aircraft, and aerial platforms. GIS, on the other hand, provides a framework for integrating, analyzing, and visualizing these geospatial data . These tools form a powerful combination that can be leveraged to address key challenges in the energy sector.

Enríquez Zárate et al. (2022) applied A.I. to detect and analyze erosion in wind turbine blades using machine learning models. The study focused on the leading-edge erosion and its impact on aerodynamic performance and structural integrity. They utilized QBlade software for aerodynamic and modal analysis, simulating different erosion levels and their effects on power generation. The researchers developed machine learning models to classify the location of erosion and predict its severity, achieving high accuracy. This innovative approach, enhanced by AutoML—which automates the process of selecting optimal models and tuning hyperparameters— provides a comprehensive method for predictive maintenance, minimizing downtime, and enhancing wind turbine efficiency.

Muxica et al. (2024) applied A.I. in remote sensing within the energy sector by designing and implementing an autonomous sensor system for vibration measurement in low-capacity wind turbines. This system, deployed on wind turbines operating under harsh weather conditions, uses A.I. to process data collected from triaxial accelerometers attached to the blades. The A.I. processes enable real-time monitoring and evaluation of the dynamic characteristics of wind turbine blades, facilitating early damage detection and maintenance. By integrating A.I. with remote sensing technologies, the system ensures reliable and efficient wind turbine operation, reducing maintenance costs and enhancing the overall reliability of wind energy 💬️ generation. This application demonstrates the potential of A.I. in advancing structural health monitoring and optimizing renewable energy resources.

To conclude, the integration of A.I. with remote sensing and GIS applications holds immense potential for advancing environmental conservation, climate adaptation, and renewable energy optimization. This research demonstrates the diverse applications of A.I. in monitoring environmental changes, predicting erosion in wind turbine blades, and enhancing the efficiency and reliability of wind energy generation. These advancements underscore the critical role of A.I. in facilitating data-driven decision-making, enabling proactive maintenance, and supporting sustainable development in the energy sector. As A.I. continues to evolve, its applications in remote sensing and GIS will undoubtedly become even more integral to addressing the current pressing environmental and energy challenges.

content.title: Case Study: Philippines
content.subtitle: AI-powered precision targeting for poverty reduction – Satellite imagery and machine learning unlocking granular poverty maps to drive emergency aid to 162,000 filipino households during COVID-19

content.text: Extreme poverty remains an ever-growing problem in the Philippines. In 2021, the magnitude of the impoverished population was 19,902,750, representing an increase of 2,232,540 or 12.6% compared to 2018, largely due to the economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic. As a result, approximately 1.6 million households in the country had no access to electricity, contributing to persistent challenges in poverty alleviation and equitable access to basic services.

To help solve these issues, UNDP Philippines, through its Accelerator Lab (ALab), implemented initiatives to support poverty eradication and address social inequality, but was challenged by the unavailability of robust, granular data to make strategies and high-level decisions (UNDP). Traditional poverty statistics compiled by <ai prompt="Tell me more about national statistical offices.">national statistical offices 💬️</ai> are available at national, regional, or provincial levels and are insufficient for training algorithms to successfully predict poverty at the granular geographic levels needed for targeted interventions (Development Asia, 2020).

UNDP Philippines, through its Accelerator Lab, has been collaborating with Zero Extreme Poverty Philippines 2030 (ZEP2030) to design and test a portfolio of approaches to localized, targeted, and convergent poverty action (UNDP, 2021). ZEP2030 is a coalition of 140 civil society organizations that have adopted the target of emancipating 1 million extremely poor families from poverty through collective action by 2030 (UNDP, 2021). To support this ambitious goal, Thinking Machines helped UNDP and Zero Extreme Poverty PH 2030 implement advanced AI-driven poverty mapping methodologies, while the Asian Development Bank separately conducted pioneering feasibility studies on using satellite imagery and machine learning for poverty estimation (UNDP Digital X).

This project aims to use machine learning and satellite imagery to map poverty in the Philippines, specifically to overcome the challenges of collecting reliable socioeconomic data that is relatively time-consuming, labor-intensive, and expensive. The project’s main objectives include using transfer learning and satellite imagery to map poverty in the country, developing preliminary poverty prediction models for the Philippines, and overcoming the limitations of traditional on-ground surveys by leveraging machine learning and geospatial information (Thinking Machines, 2019).

Data Sources and Collection

The project utilized the 2017 National Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS) as ground truth data for training machine learning models. The Philippine Statistics Authority implemented this nationwide survey from August to October 2017, covering over 31,000 households across more than 1,200 locations throughout the Philippines. The datasets include the country’s household wealth scores based on attributes such as roof material, appliance ownership, and access to water and electricity (Thinking Machines, 2019, para. 5).

The study utilized publicly available satellite imagery to ensure cost-effectiveness and broad accessibility (ResearchGate, 2019). The project used the Google Static Maps API to download 400x400 px zoom 17 satellite images, ultimately downloading 134,540 satellite images that captured detailed physical and infrastructural features (ResearchGate, 2019).

The project employed a transfer learning methodology originally developed by Stanford University researchers. This approach addressed a fundamental challenge in poverty mapping: the insufficient availability of labeled poverty data at granular geographic levels needed for training machine learning algorithms (Development Asia, 2020).

Traditional poverty statistics are typically compiled only at national, regional, or provincial levels, making it difficult to train algorithms for fine-grained poverty prediction. The transfer learning approach circumvented this limitation by using nighttime light intensity as an intermediate training target.

The project employed a transfer learning methodology originally developed by Stanford University researchers. The methodology implemented a two-stage machine learning process.
Stage 1: Nighttime Light Prediction

Researchers trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict nighttime light intensity from daytime satellite images. This leveraged the relationship between nighttime luminosity and economic development, where brighter areas typically indicate higher levels of economic activity.
Stage 2: Poverty Prediction

The team extracted 4,096-dimensional feature vectors from the trained CNN, representing visual patterns associated with different levels of nighttime light intensity. These features were then used in ridge regression models to predict household wealth and poverty levels (Thinking Machines, 2019, para. 9). With this combination of machine learning and geospatial data, they were able to provide more accurate and detailed poverty estimates across the country.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, ZEP2030 and UNDP ALab, in collaboration with startup AI4Gov, launched COVID Pulse PH. This innovative survey was deployed through a messenger chatbot that was socialized through the community networks of ZEP2030 as well as of the Philippine Rural Reconstruction Movement. Three waves of the survey were implemented since May 2020, confirming that COVID-19 affected the poorest the most (Kapi Capistrano, 2021).
Outcomes and Impact

content.body: Successfully created poverty prediction models explaining 56% of wealth variance, demonstrating the feasibility of AI-driven poverty mapping in the Philippines.
Applied poverty mapping techniques to support COVID-19 emergency food distribution targeting in Metro Manila and nearby provinces, serving 162,000 households across 44 barangays.
Established collaborative framework between UNDP Philippines Accelerator Lab and ZEP2030 coalition, leading to local convergence initiatives in areas including Antipolo City and Cebu province
Deployed COVID Pulse PH chatbot survey across three waves since May 2020, collecting real-time poverty impact data from Metro Manila, Metro Cebu, and six provinces during the pandemic
Published open-source code and methodologies, enabling replication and adaptation of the approach for other developing countries and research institutions.

content.text: The Philippines’ pioneering experience with AI-driven poverty mapping offers critical insights for other nations facing similar data scarcity and development challenges:

content.title: Scalability and Efficiency
content.body: The main lesson learned from the project demonstrates that machine learning provides a scalable, reliable, and low-cost means to obtain poverty information for areas that surveys do not cover. Traditional on-the-ground surveys can cost tens of millions of pesos and are usually done only every three to five years at the regional or provincial level, while machine learning approaches using satellite imagery offer a low-cost alternative for providing reliable estimates of poverty.

content.title: Alternative Data Approaches and Rapid Implementation
content.body: The low cost of this approach allows for rapid iteration, which opens the door to future experiments with other datasets such as road networks, population density, and mobility. The methodology can estimate wealth and poverty for any 18 square kilometer area within a fraction of the time and cost of running a household survey. With this approach, this kind of project can be rolled out to other geographies, considering its efficiency in providing results at a lower cost compared to conventional randomized surveys

content.title: Multi-Stakeholder Collaboration
content.body: The success of the project hinged on robust partnerships between UNDP Philippines Accelerator Lab, civil society coalitions such as ZEP2030, government agencies, and technology firms.

content.title: Community Validation and Local Leadership
content.body: The ZEP2030 coalition’s ‘all-in local’ strategy emphasized the importance of local leadership in poverty reduction initiatives, with local convergences serving as vehicles for poverty reduction in localities by facilitating tighter collaboration among development actors.

Data visualization can effectively bring data to life and tell a story. It is important to use data visualizations that turn information and data into actionable insights . In the energy sector, where data have an important role in justifying and rationalizing decision making, an effective visualization can enhance clarity and comprehensibility, whereas an ineffective visualization can cause confusion and loss of focus. There isn’t a global standardized framework on data visualization, however there is guidance on best principles, which come from years of research and experimentation in the design and media industries. Guidance on best practice can be found in the book Visualizing Data and in the webpage Material Design. Both references explain the correct use of graphs, the use of annotations and elements of editorial design.

takeaways.title: Exploratory Data Analysis powered by AI revolutionizes energy data insights.
takeaways.description: AI-driven EDA accelerates the identification of patterns, anomalies, and correlations in energy datasets, enabling more efficient data cleaning, clustering, and anomaly detection. By automating these processes, AI allows energy analysts to uncover critical insights—such as seasonal energy demand trends or equipment malfunctions—faster and with greater precision, optimizing energy system performance.

takeaways.title: AI-enhanced remote sensing and GIS transform energy infrastructure planning.
takeaways.description: Integrating AI with remote sensing and GIS technologies enables advanced spatial analysis, predictive maintenance, and real-time monitoring of energy assets. Applications like erosion detection in wind turbine blades and poverty mapping through satellite imagery demonstrate how AI can drive data-driven decision-making, improve renewable energy efficiency, and address energy access challenges in underserved regions.

takeaways.title: Data visualization is a strategic tool for actionable energy insights.
takeaways.description: Effective data visualization transforms complex energy data into clear, actionable narratives, enhancing decision-making and stakeholder communication. By adhering to best practices in design and storytelling, energy professionals can create visualizations that highlight key trends, such as energy consumption patterns or infrastructure performance, ensuring data-driven strategies are both accessible and impactful.
